Sometimes there is no answer to learn from: hundreds of CTD profiles and no water-mass
classification, or counts of two dozen taxa at every station and no list of the habitats
they come from. Unsupervised methods look for structure in the data itself, and they
return an answer for any table, so checking what they find matters as much as finding
it. This section works on a community matrix of taxon counts from the same simulated
survey as the rest of the course. The first three pages cover clustering:

- **clustering with k-means**: k-means sorts the stations into a set number of groups,
  each round making them tighter, and where it ends depends on where it starts;
- **choosing the number of clusters**: the sum of squares always falls as groups are
  added, so the silhouette width and a shuffled copy of the data with the groups removed
  judge how many to keep;
- **hierarchical clustering**: a tree of joins holds every number of groups at once, the
  linkage rule decides what it finds, and the adjusted Rand index scores how far two
  groupings agree.

The next two cover components:

- **principal component analysis**: new axes built from the columns make a map of the
  stations, read from their loadings, on which nothing makes an axis line up with one
  driver;
- **how many components to keep**: a set share of the variance keeps noise as well,
  parallel analysis keeps the components that hold structure, and cross-validation keeps
  those a model needs; UMAP makes a map for looking at.

The last page checks what the others found:

- **checking a pattern before reporting it**: a pattern should come back in bootstrap
  samples, leave a gap between its groups rather than cut a gradient, and match a
  recorded variable the method never saw.

The section picks up threads from earlier ones.
[Types of learning](../01-introduction/types-of-learning.qmd) ran k-means on
temperature, salinity and depth; [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd) runs it on
species counts and shows why one run is not enough.
[Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd) put the columns on a
common scale; every method in this section measures distance or spread, so each needs it.
[Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) chose a
setting by cross-validation, and [Avoiding information
leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd) kept each step inside the folds;
[How many components to keep](dimensionality-reduction.qmd) tunes the number of
components the same way. [Uncertainty and
stability](../07-validation/uncertainty-and-stability.qmd) resampled the sites to put an
interval on a score; [Checking a pattern before reporting it](interpreting-patterns.qmd)
resamples them to see whether a grouping comes back.

## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [tidyclust](https://tidyclust.tidymodels.org/), tidymodels. Clustering in the same specification and workflow idiom as the rest of the course.
- [Clustering](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html), scikit-learn user guide. The comparison figure near the top, showing ten methods on the same six datasets, is worth more than the text.
- [Decomposing signals in components](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/decomposition.html), scikit-learn user guide. PCA and its relatives.
